summary: Defines the DNAME resource record, which maps an entire subtree of the DNS name space to another domain. It was replaced by RFC 6672.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a sign that says everything under this street name has moved to a different street.

subtitle: A DNS record that redirects a whole subtree of names to another domain, not just one name.

tldr.problem: A CNAME maps only a single node of the DNS name space, so renumbering a network or renaming an organization means reconfiguring many records.
tldr.mechanism: The DNAME record (type code 39) substitutes its target for its owner as a suffix of a domain name, redirecting the entire subtree below it. Servers and resolvers get modified algorithms, and servers may synthesize CNAMEs for older clients.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2672 has been obsoleted by RFC 6672, and was updated by RFC 4592 and RFC 6604.

today: RFC 2672 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 6672. It was also updated by RFC 4592 and RFC 6604.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
The DNAME record was conceived to ease maintaining address-to-name mappings when a network is renumbered. Without it, the authoritative server for the address-to-name mappings of a network has to be reconfigured on renumbering. With DNAME, the zone can be built so that it needs no change.

It also helps in other cases, such as when an organizational unit is renamed. Unlike a CNAME, which maps a single node, DNAME maps an entire subtree of the name space to another domain.
sections.plainLanguage: If a whole neighborhood changes its name, you put up one sign at the entrance instead of changing every mailbox.

sections.title: The DNAME Resource Record
sections.content:
DNAME has the mnemonic DNAME and type code 39 (decimal). Its format is <owner> <ttl> <class> DNAME <target>, it is not class-sensitive, all fields are required, and the target is a domain name. The effect is to substitute the record's target for its owner as a suffix of a domain name.

A no-descendants rule applies: if a DNAME is present at node N, there may be other data at N (except a CNAME or another DNAME), but there MUST be no data at any descendant of N. This keeps results predictable when a non-authoritative server caches the record, and it MUST be enforced when authoritative zone data is loaded. In practice, DNAME and NS records can only coexist at the top of a zone that has only one node.

Name compression MUST NOT be applied to the DNAME RDATA unless the sender knows the receiver understands the record. Naming loops are possible, as with CNAME, so resolvers MUST limit the resources they spend on a query, though fairly long DNAME chains may be valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The record says 'swap this ending for that ending'. The one strict rule is that nothing else may live underneath the sign, so the swap always works the same way.

sections.title: Query Processing by Servers and Resolvers
sections.content:
The name resolution algorithms of RFC 1034 are changed slightly. A server checks for a DNAME before checking for a wildcard label. When a label cannot be matched, it looks at the last matched node for a DNAME, copies that record into the answer, performs the substitution and starts again. If the substituted name would overflow the legal size of a domain name, the server sets RCODE to YXDOMAIN.

Clients using EDNS0 with Version 0, or no extension at all, are presumed not to understand DNAME. For them a server SHOULD synthesize a CNAME for each DNAME encountered. That CNAME MUST have the same class as the query, a TTL of zero, an owner equal to the QNAME in effect at that moment, and RDATA holding the new name. A server with the key on-line MAY also sign the synthesized CNAME.

A resolver treats DNAME as somewhat like CNAME: it caches the DNAME, substitutes the target for the owner in the name being resolved and starts over. If the result would be too long, it returns an implementation-dependent error. A resolver that understands DNAME but sends non-extended queries MUST drop any CNAME in the reply whose owner is a subdomain of a DNAME owner in that reply.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer looks up a name and finds the sign, it rewrites the name using the new street and asks again. Older computers that cannot read the sign get a note saying the answer was rewritten.

sections.title: Examples of Use
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. In organizational renaming, if FROBOZZ.EXAMPLE joins ACME.EXAMPLE, the old zone can hold a DNAME pointing at frobozz-division.acme.example. to ease the transition.

In classless delegation of shorter prefixes, the scheme for in-addr.arpa delegation can be extended to prefixes shorter than 24 bits. The example delegates the prefix 192.0.8.0/22 with an NS record plus DNAME records for 8, 9, 10 and 11.

In network renumbering support, DNAME records could replace NS records for delegation so that the address space of an ISP can change without altering the zone files that describe its use. The RFC admits that renumbering IPv4 is so laborious that updating the DNS is a small part of it, so the value may be low, and it hopes DNAME will be more useful with IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: A company that merges with another can leave a forwarding sign at its old address, and a network that changes numbers can keep its phone book unchanged.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content: The DNAME type code 39 and its name had already been registered with IANA. On security, DNAME is like CNAME if a spoofed record is inserted into a server or resolver. The difference is that its effect covers a whole subtree of the name space. The facilities of DNSSEC are available to authenticate this record type.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake sign would be worse than a fake note on one door, because it would redirect a whole street. Locks on the signs exist to stop that.
